big_case_rationale: Decides whether every employee of a federally funded school or university may sue under Title IX for sex discrimination in employment, resolving an 8-3 circuit split and reshaping implied-right-of-action doctrine; broad institutional reach, though Title VII remains available to most of the affected workers.

semantic_claims.proposition: The majority will hold that Title IX's implied private right of action (Cannon, as ratified in 42 U.S.C. 2000d-7) does not reach an employee's claim of sex discrimination in employment, on the ground that the scope of an implied remedy is a question of Congress's remedial intent analytically distinct from the reach of the substantive prohibition (Sandoval, Gonzaga, Virginia Bankshares), so North Haven v. Bell's holding that section 901 covers employment does not carry the remedy; the decisive structural inference is that Congress extended Title VII's comprehensive remedial scheme to educational employers weeks before enacting Title IX, which forecloses a parallel, procedure-free Title IX remedy for the same claims (Novotny, Northwest Airlines, Brown v. GSA). Jackson v. Birmingham is distinguished as a retaliation claim unavailable under Title VII, not overruled, and ratification is rejected because no pre-1986 decision of the Court recognized the employee claim.

The majority's stated ground will be categorical, not fact-bound: no employee of a funding recipient has an implied Title IX right of action for sex discrimination in the terms and conditions of their own employment, whatever the plaintiff's actual access to Title VII (the Court will not carve out student-employees, sub-15-employee institutions, or time-barred Title VII claimants, treating those gaps as Congress's to fill), while expressly leaving intact Cannon's student right of action, Jackson's retaliation claim, and the government's funding-termination remedy for employment discrimination under North Haven.
